+ --> src/mdtest_snippet.py:2:8
+  |
+2 | import foo.bar as bar  # snapshot: manual-from-import
+  |        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
+help: Replace with `from foo import bar`
+  |
+1 | __lazy_modules__ = ["foo", "foo.bar"]
+  - import foo.bar as bar  # snapshot: manual-from-import
+2 + from foo import bar  # snapshot: manual-from-import
+  |
+```
+
+## Only the submodule listed
+
+A `from` import checks its containing module for membership in `__lazy_modules__`. Rewriting this
+import would make it eager, so the diagnostic has no fix.
+
+```py
+__lazy_modules__ = ["foo.bar"]
+import foo.bar as bar  # snapshot: manual-from-import
+```
+
+```snapshot
+error[PLR0402]: Use `from foo import bar` in lieu of alias
+ --> src/mdtest_snippet.py:2:8
+  |
+2 | import foo.bar as bar  # snapshot: manual-from-import
+  |        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
+help: Replace with `from foo import bar`
+```
+
+## Only the package listed
+
+Listing a package does not make imports of its submodules lazy. Rewriting this import would make it
+lazy, so the diagnostic has no fix.
+
+```py
+__lazy_modules__ = ["foo"]
+import foo.bar as bar  # snapshot: manual-from-import
+```
+
+```snapshot
+error[PLR0402]: Use `from foo import bar` in lieu of alias
+ --> src/mdtest_snippet.py:2:8
+  |
+2 | import foo.bar as bar  # snapshot: manual-from-import
+  |        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
+help: Replace with `from foo import bar`
+```
+
+## Explicit lazy imports
+
+The fix preserves the `lazy` keyword, so the import remains lazy even when the package is absent
+from `__lazy_modules__`.
+
+```py
+__lazy_modules__ = ["foo.bar"]
+lazy import foo.bar as bar  # snapshot: manual-from-import
+```
+

+error[PLR0402]: Use `from foo import bar` in lieu of alias
+ --> src/mdtest_snippet.py:2:13

+help: Replace with `from foo import bar`
+  |
+1 | __lazy_modules__ = ["foo.bar"]
+  - lazy import foo.bar as bar  # snapshot: manual-from-import
+2 + lazy from foo import bar  # snapshot: manual-from-import
+  |
+```
+
+## Unknown declarations
+
+When the declaration's contents are unknown, the rule cannot establish whether the fix preserves
+laziness, so no fix is offered.
+
+```py
+__lazy_modules__ = configured_lazy_modules

+```

+  |
+2 | import foo.bar as bar  # snapshot: manual-from-import
+  |        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

+```

+
+Imports inside functions are eager regardless of `__lazy_modules__`, so an unknown declaration does

+Pydantic allows a frozen model to be subclassed and then made mutable again. This is generally

+emitting any errors:

I do think it is reasonable to make assumptions about how dunders work, and in practice ty does do this:

```

I also noticed ty's handling of fixed length tuples of Any is a little weird, or at least it differs from all the other type checkers:
```
from typing import Any

def f1():
    x: tuple[int, int, int] = (0, 1, 2)
    x += (1, 2, 3)  # error
    reveal_type(x)  # tuple[int, int, int]

def f2():
    x: tuple[Any, Any, Any] = (0, 1, 2)
    x += (1, 2, 3)  # no error
    reveal_type(x)  # tuple[Any, ...]
```

It doesn't answer any of your other questions, but we concluded that for the specific example of tuple addition, it's probably not worth sacrificing correctness, given that there is a decent workaround:
```py
def f(x: tuple[int, int]) -> tuple[str, int, int]:
    return ("asdf", *x)
```

I filed https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/3430 to specifically track the weird tuple-of-Any issue, since that's distinct.

I do think it's inconsistent that we are willing to infer precise types for slicing of tuples and iteration of tuples, even though those can both also be overridden (without Liskov violation), but then we don't in other cases. It seems to me that we should have a consistent story here -- either we account for the possibility of overridden dunders in subclasses with odd behavior, or we don't.

I'm sorry to re-add to our needs-decision issue count, but personally I find that argument strong enough to reopen this.

I went to fix https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/3430 and realized that it's not a distinct issue at all. It directly derives from this issue. We don't special-case tuple addition, we just fall back on`tuple.__add__` from typeshed, which makes everything fall back to unioned homogenous variable-length tuple types. This results in differing behavior for fixed-length tuple types where every element is dynamic, because the homogenous variable-length upcast of `tuple[Any, Any, Any]` is `tuple[Any, ...]`, which has special gradual behavior (per the type spec), unlike any other `tuple[T, ...]`.

So that behavior is all expected -- I don't really see any clean fix for the `tuple[Any, Any, Any]` problem without more generally adding the tuple-addition precision.

Since I was already trying to fix https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/3430, I now have a PR for this, and the impact in our test suite looks pretty positive. Will go ahead and push it up and see what it looks like on the ecosystem.

In light of other decisions we've made since in similar areas, it seems quite clear to me at this point that "a subclass might override `__add__` in a weird way" is not sufficient rationale to not do this; we should just assume they don't do that.

I think the real blocker here (and the reason the PR mentioned in my last comment didn't go anywhere back then) is that more precise tuple addition can cause new divergent inference of implicit instance attributes (e.g. `self.x = self.x + (1,)` leading to an ever-expanding tuple type). But it would be worth trying again, our handling of those cases has improved some I think.

`TC001` - `TC003` should not apply with lazy imports

### Summary

[PEP 810 (Explicit lazy imports)](https://peps.python.org/pep-0810/) specifically calls out lazy imports as [eliminat[ing] the common need for `TYPE_CHECKING` guards](https://peps.python.org/pep-0810/#what-about-type-annotations-and-type-checking-imports). While `TYPE_CHECKING` may still have a use for avoiding circular imports, it's does cause a lot of issues for tools that rely on runtime behavior (think: [sphinx.ext.autodoc](https://www.sphinx-doc.org/en/master/usage/extensions/autodoc.html), [beartype](https://github.com/beartype/beartype), etc.). Would it make sense to deprecate these rules or discourage their use code bases that only support Python 3.15 or greater, on the basis that users would be better off using lazy imports to avoid these expensive imports?
hints:
I think it would be a bit early to deprecate these rules since Ruff supports much older Python versions than 3.15, but it does make sense to me to adjust the rules to account for lazy imports, for example by suggesting a `lazy` import instead of moving to a `TYPE_CHECKING` block on 3.15 or later.

Agreed with adjusting the rules, though we could also deprecate the rules outright if [`target-version` or `project.requires-python`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#src) indicated that the project under test only supported >= 3.15. That's what I was getting at with "[w]ould it make sense to deprecate these rules or discourage their use code bases **that only support Python 3.15 or greater**". At some point many (5 1/2?) years from now this will be true for everyone 😄

Playing devil's advocate here, should you make sure the user has opted-in to lazy imports before silently stopping to apply those rules?

My immediate plan for this issue was to add another fix option that suggests `lazy` imports on 3.15+ instead of one of the other fixes, not to stop applying the rules.

Better diagnostic to help users annotate async generator in stub

### Summary

Consider the example:

```py
from collections.abc import AsyncGenerator
import aiofiles

class AsyncTest:
    async def __call__(self, path: str) -> AsyncGenerator[str]:
        async with aiofiles.open(path) as f:
            async for line in f:
                yield line

async def test() -> None:
    test: AsyncTest = AsyncTest()
    items: list[str] = [item async for item in test('/')]
```

Ty does not complain about anything here, as it shouldn't. But if I replace the `__call__` function with a stub:

```py
class AsyncTest:
    async def __call__(self, path: str) -> AsyncGenerator[str]: ...

async def test() -> None:
    test: AsyncTest = AsyncTest()
    items: list[str] = [item async for item in test('/')]
```

Then, on the last line, ty reports an error: Object of type `CoroutineType[Any, Any, AsyncGenerator[str, None]]` is not async-iterable.

I assume that in the first case, ty can see the `yield` in the function body, so it infers that despite the async def, this is actually an async generator function.

But per PEP 525 / typing spec: if you annotate the return type of an async generator function, you should use AsyncGenerator[YieldType, SendType] as the return annotation, and the function is understood to be an async generator (not a coroutine returning one). Therefore, ty should be able to understand the function is an async generator even in the second example.

This example passes in ty 0.0.81 and fails in 0.0.82:

```python
Capybara = list['Capybara'] | int


def hutia(gundi: Capybara) -> Capybara:
    while isinstance(gundi, list):
        gundi = gundi[0]
    return gundi
```

```console
ty check --error unsound-return-statement example.py
```

Expected: `gundi` remains a `Capybara`, and after the loop can only be an `int`. Indexing the recursive list does not introduce an untyped value.

The regression disappears if the loop becomes an `if`, or if the alias becomes nonrecursive (`list[int] | int`). query:
Exponential slowdown for captures in nested class patterns over a recursive union

### Summary

### Summary

`ty check` gets very slow when a `match` case binds a name inside nested class patterns and the class attributes are typed as a recursive union. Check time grows roughly like union size to the power of nesting depth. The slowdown started when ty added inference for class-pattern bindings in [astral-sh/ruff#25941](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/25941).

The repro is a bit constructed, but any recursive union of classes runs into this I think.

### Reproduction

```python
from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import TypeAlias


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Wrap:
    inner: Node


class Leaf0: ...
class Leaf1: ...
class Leaf2: ...
class Leaf3: ...
class Leaf4: ...
class Leaf5: ...
class Leaf6: ...
class Leaf7: ...
class Leaf8: ...
class Leaf9: ...
class Leaf10: ...
class Leaf11: ...
class Leaf12: ...
class Leaf13: ...
class Leaf14: ...
class Leaf15: ...
class Leaf16: ...
class Leaf17: ...
class Leaf18: ...
class Leaf19: ...
class Leaf20: ...
class Leaf21: ...
class Leaf22: ...
class Leaf23: ...
class Leaf24: ...



Node: TypeAlias = Wrap | Leaf0 | Leaf1 | Leaf2 | Leaf3 | Leaf4 | Leaf5 | Leaf6 | Leaf7 | Leaf8 | Leaf9 | Leaf10 | Leaf11 | Leaf12 | Leaf13 | Leaf14 | Leaf15 | Leaf16 | Leaf17 | Leaf18 | Leaf19 | Leaf20 | Leaf21 | Leaf22 | Leaf23 | Leaf24


def f(node: Node) -> None:
    match node:
        case Wrap(inner=Wrap(inner=Wrap(inner=Wrap(inner=Wrap(inner=captured))))):
            pass
```

This takes around ~15s on my machine to check.

### Related Issues

Very similar explosion I could find: https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/3880

### Experiments

Small changes prevent the slowdown:

- Replacing the capture `inner=captured` with `inner=_` reduces runtime to ~0.04s.
- Marking `Wrap` as `@final` reduces runtime to ~0.04s.
- A single level of nesting, `case Wrap(inner=captured)`, takes ~0.05s.

Other changes make it worse:

- Adding more fields to `Wrap` (`inner2: Node`, `inner3: Node`, ...) and matching each of them at every level adds roughly the cost of a single field on top
- Runtime grows quickly with nesting depth and union size:

| leaf classes | depth 3 | depth 4 | depth 5 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8 | 0.05s | 0.08s | 0.40s |
| 16 | 0.13s | 1.5s | 24s |
| 24 | 0.63s | 15s | >300s |

+An attribute can have different types in different subclasses. A class pattern that checks the
+attribute narrows the subject to the subclass whose attribute can match:
+
+```py
+class Holder:
+    value: object
+
+class IntHolder(Holder):
+    value: int
+
+class StrHolder(Holder):
+    value: str

+def filter_holders(holder: IntHolder | StrHolder) -> None:

+```
+
+## Class patterns with multiple attributes
+
+Each attribute is narrowed by its own pattern, even when the attributes have the same type:
+
+```py
+class Pair:
+    left: int | str
+    right: int | str

+    match value:

+
+The `child` attribute is itself a `Node`, so a nested capture can be either a `Branch` or a `Leaf`:
+

+
+class Branch:
+    child: Node
+
+class Leaf: ...
+
+Node: TypeAlias = Branch | Leaf
+

+    match node:

+
+Both tuple variants have a first element of type `Node`, so the nested capture has that type:
+
+```py
+from __future__ import annotations
+from typing import Literal, TypeAlias
+
+Node: TypeAlias = tuple["Node", Literal[0]] | tuple["Node", Literal[1]] | None

+def visit(value: Node) -> None:

+
+Each alternative captures a nested `child`, while the `as` pattern binds the value matched by the
+whole pattern:

+from typing import TypeAlias

query:
Inhomogeneous tuple-item narrowing only seems to work with equivalence-relation checks

### Summary

(Playground: https://play.ty.dev/70c43888-ebf3-414c-b9e4-7ab8626386e3)

Summary
----
Narrowing of other items in inhomogeneous tuples based on an item doesn't seem to work for common cases like instance and truth-value checks.

The confirmed good cases are all equivalence-relation checks (`is` and `==`), so IDK if those are only working because they are somehow special-cased.

Examples
----
`ty` narrows the items in unions of inhomogeneous tuples for quite a few cases:
```python
from collections.abc import Callable
from typing import Literal, reveal_type


def narrowing_by_identity(
    foo: tuple[int, Callable[[int], int]] | tuple[None, Callable[[], int]],
) -> int:
    if foo[0] is None:
        return reveal_type(foo[1])()  # Callable[[], int]
    return reveal_type(foo[1])(foo[0])  # Callable[[int], int]


def narrowing_by_literal_compare(
    foo: (
        tuple[Literal[True], Callable[[int], int]]
        | tuple[Literal[False], Callable[[], int]]
    ),
) -> int:
    if foo[0] == True:  # The linter's probably won't like this...
        return reveal_type(foo[1])(1)  # Callable[[int], int]
    return reveal_type(foo[1])()  # Callable[[], int]
```
For example, the above cases both type-check.

However, cases like truth-value and instance checks don't seem to be covered:
```python
def no_narrowing_by_instance_check(
    foo: tuple[int, Callable[[int], int]] | tuple[str, Callable[[], int]],
) -> int:
    if isinstance(foo[0], str):
        return reveal_type(foo[1])()  # Callable[[], int]
    return reveal_type(foo[1])(foo[0])  # Callable[[int], int]


def no_narrowing_by_truth_value(
    foo: (
        tuple[Literal[True], Callable[[int], int]]
        | tuple[Literal[False], Callable[[], int]]
    ),
) -> int:
    # Since `foo[0]` is a bool-literal, it should be safe to assume
    # `foo[0] == (foo[0] == True)` in all cases
    if foo[0]:
        return reveal_type(foo[1])(1)  # Callable[[int], int]
    return reveal_type(foo[1])()  # Callable[[], int]
```
Narrowing on `foo[1]`  is lost on both the above cases (as shown by the `reveal_type()` calls printing out unions instead of the expected `Callable[...]`) and thus `ty` complains about the calls.

- In the former case, it seems that the errors are not due to caution against intersection types and/or multiple inheritance; I tried inserting `if TYPE_CHECKING: assert not isinstance(foo[0], <the_other_type>)` inside the branches and the errors persisted.
- The latter case is especially egregious (and really what inspired the issue), since `if <bool>: ...` is idiomatic, while `if <bool> == True: ...` is proscribed. If my assumption that the equivalence-relation checks are special-cased is correct, may I suggest that truth-value checks on common values (esp. `Literal[True, False]`) also be special-cased. (Of course it would be nice to fix this in general, but maybe there are other concerns.)

Notes
----
`mypy` handles all the above cases correctly: the `reveal_type()` calls print the expected outputs, and the code type-checks. No idea about other type-checkers though.

 ```
 
+### Tuple unions and truthiness
+
+A truthiness check on one tuple element can narrow the other elements.
+
+```py
+from typing import Literal
+
+def truthy(value: tuple[Literal[True], int] | tuple[Literal[False], str]):
+    if value[0]:
+        reveal_type(value[1])  # revealed: int
+    else:
+        reveal_type(value[1])  # revealed: str
+```
+
+Negating the check selects the tuple with the falsy element. Negative indices work too:
+
+```py
+def negated(value: tuple[Literal[True], int] | tuple[Literal[False], str]):
+    if not value[-2]:
+        reveal_type(value[1])  # revealed: str
+```
+
+Calling `bool` on the element has the same effect as checking its truthiness directly:
+
+```py
+def explicit_bool(value: tuple[Literal[True], int] | tuple[Literal[False], str]):
+    if bool(value[0]):
+        reveal_type(value[1])  # revealed: int
+```
+
+The checked element can also be a union of literals that are all truthy or all falsy:
+
+```py
+def literal_tags(value: tuple[Literal[0, ""], str] | tuple[Literal[1, "x"], int]):
+    if value[0]:
+        reveal_type(value[1])  # revealed: int
+    else:
+        reveal_type(value[1])  # revealed: str
+```
+
+A `bool` element can be either true or false, so its tuple remains possible in both branches:
+
+```py
+def ambiguous(value: tuple[bool, int] | tuple[Literal[False], str]):
+    if value[0]:
+        reveal_type(value)  # revealed: tuple[bool, int]
+    else:
+        reveal_type(value)  # revealed: tuple[bool, int] | tuple[Literal[False], str]
+```
+
+### Tuple unions and instance checks
+
+An `isinstance` check on one element narrows the other elements in both branches.
+
+```py
+def instance(value: tuple[int, str] | tuple[str, int]):
+    if isinstance(value[0], str):
+        reveal_type(value[1])  # revealed: int
+    else:
+        reveal_type(value[1])  # revealed: str
+```
+
+An `int | str` element can pass or fail the `str` check, so its tuple remains possible in both
+branches:
+
+```py
+def overlapping(value: tuple[int | str, bytes] | tuple[str, int]):
+    if isinstance(value[0], str):
+        reveal_type(value)  # revealed: tuple[int | str, bytes] | tuple[str, int]
+    else:
+        reveal_type(value)  # revealed: tuple[int | str, bytes]
+```
+
+### Tuple unions and subclass checks
+
+Subclass checks also narrow the tuple containing the checked class.
+
+```py
+def subclass(value: tuple[type[int], str] | tuple[type[str], int]):
+    if issubclass(value[0], str):
+        reveal_type(value[1])  # revealed: int
+    else:
+        reveal_type(value[1])  # revealed: str
+```
+
+### Tuple unions and `TypeIs`
+
+A user-defined `TypeIs` check narrows the tuple containing its argument.
+
+```py
+from typing_extensions import TypeIs
+
+def is_string(value: object) -> TypeIs[str]:
+    return isinstance(value, str)
+
+def check(value: tuple[int, str] | tuple[str, int]):
+    if is_string(value[0]):
+        reveal_type(value[1])  # revealed: int
+    else:
+        reveal_type(value[1])  # revealed: str
+```
+
+The checked element can be passed by keyword:
+
+```py
+def keyword(value: tuple[int, str] | tuple[str, int]):
+    if is_string(value=value[0]):
+        reveal_type(value[1])  # revealed: int
+```
+
+### Tuple unions and `TypeGuard`
+
+`TypeGuard` can widen its argument's type, so it does not eliminate tuples from the union.
+
+```py
+from typing_extensions import TypeGuard
+
+def guard_string(value: object) -> TypeGuard[str]:
+    return isinstance(value, str)
+
+def check(value: tuple[int, str] | tuple[str, int]):
+    if guard_string(value[0]):
+        reveal_type(value)  # revealed: tuple[int, str] | tuple[str, int]
+```
+
+### Tuple unions with `Any` elements
+
+An `Any` element can pass or fail a truthiness or `isinstance` check, so its tuple remains possible
+in both branches.
+
+```py
+from typing import Any, Literal
+
+def check(value: tuple[Any, bytes] | tuple[Literal[False], str]):
+    if value[0]:
+        reveal_type(value)  # revealed: tuple[Any, bytes]
+    else:
+        reveal_type(value)  # revealed: tuple[Any, bytes] | tuple[Literal[False], str]
+    if isinstance(value[0], str):
+        reveal_type(value)  # revealed: tuple[Any, bytes]
+    else:
+        reveal_type(value)  # revealed: tuple[Any, bytes] | tuple[Literal[False], str]
+```
+
+### Tuple unions with other types
+
+The check can rule out a tuple while leaving other types in the union. It does not narrow those
+other types.
+
+```py
+def check(value: list[str] | tuple[int, int]):
+    if isinstance(value[0], str):
+        reveal_type(value)  # revealed: list[str]
+    else:
+        reveal_type(value)  # revealed: list[str] | tuple[int, int]
+```
+
+### Tuple unions with variable-length tuples
+
+`tuple[str, ...]` supplies a string at every valid index, so the check can distinguish it from
+`tuple[int, int]`.
+
+```py
+def check(value: tuple[str, ...] | tuple[int, int]):
+    if isinstance(value[0], str):
+        reveal_type(value)  # revealed: tuple[str, ...]
+    else:
+        reveal_type(value)  # revealed: tuple[int, int]
+```
+
+### Tuple unions with unknown indices
+
+When the index is not known, the check cannot identify which tuple is present.
+
+```py
+from typing import Literal
+
+def check(value: tuple[Literal[False], str] | tuple[str, Literal[False]], index: int):
+    if value[index]:
+        reveal_type(value)  # revealed: tuple[Literal[False], str] | tuple[str, Literal[False]]
+    if isinstance(value[index], str):
+        reveal_type(value)  # revealed: tuple[Literal[False], str] | tuple[str, Literal[False]]
+```
+
+### Tuple unions with out-of-bounds indices
+
+If the index is out of bounds for any tuple in the union, we report an error and leave the union
+unchanged.
+
+```py
+def check(value: tuple[int, str] | tuple[str]):
+    # error: [index-out-of-bounds]
+    if isinstance(value[1], str):
+        reveal_type(value)  # revealed: tuple[int, str] | tuple[str]
+    # error: [index-out-of-bounds]
+    if value[1]:
+        reveal_type(value)  # revealed: tuple[int, str] | tuple[str]
+```
+
+### Tuple checks that assign to another name
+
+Assigning the checked element to another name leaves the tuple unchanged, but currently prevents
+narrowing the tuple.
+
+```py
+def element(value: tuple[str, int] | tuple[int, str]):
+    if isinstance(item := value[0], str):
+        # TODO: Narrow to `int`.
+        reveal_type(value[1])  # revealed: int | str
+```
+
+### Tuple checks that reassign the tuple
+
+Assigning a checked element back to the tuple's name replaces the tuple. The check narrows the
+assigned element without restoring the old tuple type.
+
+```py
+def instance(flag: bool):
+    value = ("x",) if flag else (1,)
+    if isinstance(value := value[0], str):
+        reveal_type(value)  # revealed: Literal["x"]
+    else:
+        reveal_type(value)  # revealed: Literal[1]
+```
+
+The same applies to user-defined `TypeIs` checks:
+
+```py
+from typing_extensions import TypeIs
+
+def is_string(value: object) -> TypeIs[str]:
+    return isinstance(value, str)
+
+def check(flag: bool):
+    value = ("x",) if flag else (1,)
+    if is_string(value := value[0]):
+        reveal_type(value)  # revealed: Literal["x"]
+    else:
+        reveal_type(value)  # revealed: Literal[1]
+```
+
+### Tuple reassignment in an index
+
+Python reads the tuple before evaluating its index. The index expression below then replaces `value`
+with `(False,)`. The truthiness check uses the original tuple and does not narrow the replacement.
+
+```py
+from typing import Literal
+
+def check(value: tuple[Literal[True]] | tuple[Literal[False]]):
+    if value[(value := (False,)) and 0]:
+        reveal_type(value)  # revealed: tuple[Literal[False]]
+```
+
+### Tuple checks with assignments in later arguments
+
+An assignment in a later argument can replace the tuple after its element has been read. The check
+does not narrow the replacement value.
+
+```py
+from typing_extensions import TypeIs
+
+def is_string(value: object, other: object) -> TypeIs[str]:
+    return isinstance(value, str)
+
+def positional(flag: bool):
+    value = ("x",) if flag else (1,)
+    if is_string(value[0], value := 0):

query:
Equality comparisons involving intersection types incorrectly infer `Never` for non-boolean return types

### Summary

After negative `isinstance` narrowing, ty infers an equality comparison as `Never`, even though explicitly calling `__eq__` returns the expected intersection type. This also causes an enclosing `and` expression to be incorrectly inferred as `Literal[False]`.

```python
from typing import Self, reveal_type

class Index:
    def __eq__(self, other) -> Self:  # ty: ignore[invalid-method-override]
        return self

class MultiIndex: ...

def f(index: Index):
    reveal_type(index.__eq__(''))  # Index
    reveal_type(index == '')  # Index

    if not isinstance(index, MultiIndex):
        reveal_type(index)  # Index & ~MultiIndex
        reveal_type(index.__eq__(''))  # Index & ~MultiIndex
        reveal_type(index == '')  # Never

    reveal_type(not isinstance(index, MultiIndex) and index == '')  # Literal[False]
```

The last two revealed types are incorrect. The narrowed comparison should have type `Index & ~MultiIndex`, consistent with the explicit method call. The final expression should have type `Literal[False] | (Index & ~MultiIndex)`: it can return an `Index` instance, not just `False`.

### Suspected cause

Codex says:

> The [intersection-comparison fallback unconditionally adds `bool` to the result intersection](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/blob/ae4d792c6bdb3e27e88f22e6ca62bedfc767d8d3/crates/ty_python_semantic/src/types/infer/comparisons.rs#L943-L966). This appears to intersect the `Index` return type with `bool`, producing `Never`.
> 
> Equality comparisons can return non-boolean objects, so restricting the result to `bool` is incorrect here.

+    reveal_type("ready" != value)  # revealed: Literal[True]

This is a case where ty is doing what the typing spec actually says to do (and the strictly correct thing to do), whereas all other type checkers have decided to implement some heuristic to favor the first overload and depart from what the spec actually says.

Specifically, mypy and pyrefly both exclude `self` arguments (bound method receiver) from step 5 of the overload algorithm. (I don't see any principled reason why these arguments should be excluded). Pyright goes further than this and often prefers the first overload rather than applying step 5 of the specified algorithm at all.

It seems to me that ty's inference here is more correct than any other type checker. If you have a `Series[Any]` and call `__sub__` on it, there's no reason to assume it must be a `Series[Timestamp]` just because that overload happens to come first. The ideal return type here would be `AnyOf[Timestamp, Timedelta]` -- `Any` or `Unknown` is the best available option short of having an `AnyOf` type.

That said, we could easily implement the same approach as mypy/pyrefly for compatibility's sake.

https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/27054 implements the same approach as mypy/pyrefly, for evaluation purposes.

Following python/mypy#22011, nightly mypy now also recognises the gradual receiver ambiguity. Rather than restoring first-match selection, could ty preserve the shared outer container where possible? This would give pandas-stubs a migration path.

+@overload

+@overload

PERF401/PERF403 fixes introduce a syntax error when the loop iterable is a ternary expression

### Summary

The preview fixes for [`manual-list-comprehension` (PERF401)](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/manual-list-comprehension/) and [`manual-dict-comprehension` (PERF403)](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/manual-dict-comprehension/) introduce a syntax error when the `for` loop iterates over an unparenthesized conditional expression. A comprehension's iterable can't be a bare ternary, so it needs parentheses there.

```console
$ cat >perf401.py <<'# EOF'
def f(values, allowed):
    found = []
    for value in [values] if isinstance(values, str) else values:
        if value not in allowed:
            found.append(value)
    return found
# EOF

$ ruff --isolated check perf401.py --select PERF401 --preview --unsafe-fixes --diff 2>&1 | grep error:
error: Fix introduced a syntax error. Reverting all changes.

$ cat >perf403.py <<'# EOF'
def f(values):
    result = {}
    for key, value in [values] if isinstance(values, tuple) else values:
        result[key] = value
    return result
# EOF

$ ruff --isolated check perf403.py --select PERF403 --preview --unsafe-fixes --diff 2>&1 | grep error:
error: Fix introduced a syntax error. Reverting all changes.
```

For PERF401 the generated code is `found.extend(value for value in [values] if isinstance(values, str) else values if value not in allowed)`; the valid form is `found.extend(value for value in ([values] if isinstance(values, str) else values) if value not in allowed)`.

#18405 added parentheses around a lambda or ternary *condition*. The *iterable* is still only parenthesized when it is an implicit tuple, in both [`manual_list_comprehension.rs`](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/blob/95201641dc6add3471d404efcfeb3b4d1b9d3372/crates/ruff_linter/src/rules/perflint/rules/manual_list_comprehension.rs#L392-L408) and [`manual_dict_comprehension.rs`](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/blob/95201641dc6add3471d404efcfeb3b4d1b9d3372/crates/ruff_linter/src/rules/perflint/rules/manual_dict_comprehension.rs#L335-L350). A named expression as the iterable fails the same way: `for value in (items := values):` with the PERF401 fix also reports the syntax error.

Without `--preview` the PERF401 violation is reported but no fix is offered.

### Version

ruff 0.16.10 (also reproduced with 0.16.3; the code linked above is from `main` at 95201641dc6a)

query:
Stack overflow on syntax error indexing of list of recursive typevar union complement

### Summary

This code:
```py
from typing import reveal_type
from ty_extensions import Intersection, Not

type A = list[Not[A] | A]

def foo(x: A):
    reveal_type(x[])
```
Causes a stack overflow like this `thread '<unknown>' (67524) has overflowed its stack` and crashes the playground.

The code is very suspect for a few reasons:
Just revealing the type without the indexing gives `list[~A | A]`, which should be equal to `list[object]`, but I suspect because of `list`'s invariance is incorrectly not being simplified out
```py
PS ~>echo @'
from typing import reveal_type
from ty_extensions import Intersection, Not

type A = list[Not[A] | A]

def foo(x: A):
    reveal_type(x)
'@ > issue.py
PS ~>uvx ty check issue.py
info[revealed-type]: Revealed type
 --> issue.py:7:17
  |
6 | def foo(x: A):
7 |     reveal_type(x)
  |                 ^ `list[~A | A]`
  |

Found 1 diagnostic
```

If the indexing is not a syntax error, the type of the elements is revealed as `~list[Any] | list[Any]`, which also should be `object`.
```py
PS ~>echo @'
from typing import reveal_type
from ty_extensions import Intersection, Not

type A = list[Not[A] | A]

def foo(x: A):
    reveal_type(x[0])
'@ > issue.py
PS ~>uvx ty check issue.py
info[revealed-type]: Revealed type
 --> issue.py:7:17
  |
6 | def foo(x: A):
7 |     reveal_type(x[0])
  |                 ^^^^ `~list[Any] | list[Any]`
  |

Found 1 diagnostic
```

### Version

ty 0.0.27 (5c9e342c2 2026-03-31)
hints:
I don't think we handle `list[Any] | ~list[Any]` correctly right now, but unfortunately I think it would also be incorrect for `list[Any] | ~list[Any]` to simplify to `object`... gradual types are weird: the two `Any`s might not materialize to the same type. There's some detailed discussion on this in https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/20651#issuecomment-3360130113.

I think we could simplify `~A | A` to `object` before `Any` ever enters the picture, though. Even `~Any | Any` is known to be `object` _if_ we know the two `Any` represent the same (unknown) type -- and that's the scenario here.

It's also strange that `Any` is even entering the picture in the first place, since the type should still involve `A`s, but I think that is an existing limitation of self-referential list types:
https://play.ty.dev/e1e74dc4-c8e2-43ed-89e4-fa884d326789
```py
from typing import reveal_type
type A = list[A]

def foo(x: A):
    # Expected: `list[A]` or `A`
    reveal_type(x[0])  # Revealed type: `list[Any]`
```

Yes, it's a current limitation of our self-referential types in general that when we transform them in any way, the point of recursion is transformed to `Any`.

+
+## Negation after specializing a recursive alias
+
+Substituting `object` for `T` makes `A[T]` equal to `object`, even though its definition is
+recursive. Its negation is therefore `Never`.
+
+```py
+from typing import TypeVar
+from typing_extensions import Never, assert_type
+from ty_extensions import Not
+
+T = TypeVar("T")
+A = T | list["A[T]"]
+
+def f(x: Not[A[object]]):
+    assert_type(x, Never)
+```
+
+Specialization can also expose two negations. They cancel, leaving the specialized list or `int`.
+
+```py
+B = Not[list["B[T]"] | T]
+
+def g(x: Not[B[int]]):
+    assert_type(x, list[B[int]] | int)
+```
+
+## Excluding a recursive alias from a list
+
+`Without[A]` describes a list that is not an `A`. Since `list[Any]` is gradual, its `Any` can stand
+for a different type in each union member. The exclusion still matters: the element type does not
+simplify to `list[Any]`.
+
+```py
+from typing import Any, TypeVar
+from typing_extensions import TypeAliasType
+from ty_extensions import Intersection, Not
+
+T = TypeVar("T")
+Without = TypeAliasType("Without", Intersection[list[Any], Not[T]], type_params=(T,))
+A = TypeAliasType("A", "list[Without[A] | A]")
+
+def f(x: A):
+    reveal_type(x[0])  # revealed: (list[Any] & ~A) | list[Without[A] | A]
+```
+
+## Excluding a recursive alias from `object`

+Here, specializing `Without` with `object` leaves just `Not[A]`. The alias `A` contains no gradual
+types, so `Without[object, A] | A` covers every object.

+```py

+from typing_extensions import TypeAliasType, assert_type
+from ty_extensions import Intersection, Not
+
+T = TypeVar("T")
+U = TypeVar("U")
+Without = TypeAliasType("Without", Intersection[T, Not[U]], type_params=(T, U))
+A = TypeAliasType("A", "list[Without[object, A] | A]")
+
+def f(x: A):
+    assert_type(x[0], object)
+```

+## Recursive tuple elements in a protocol
+
+Each element of `A` must be both another `A` and an `Items`. We can inspect an element without
+expanding the tuple indefinitely, and an integer still fails that requirement.

+```py

+from typing import Any, Protocol, TypeVar
+from typing_extensions import TypeAliasType, assert_type
+from ty_extensions import Intersection
+
+class Items(Protocol):
+    def __iter__(self) -> Iterator[Any]: ...
+
+T = TypeVar("T")
+WithItems = TypeAliasType("WithItems", Intersection[Items, T], type_params=(T,))
+A = TypeAliasType("A", "tuple[WithItems[A], ...]")
+
+def f(x: A):
+    assert_type(x[0], WithItems[A])
+    y: int = x[0]  # error: [invalid-assignment]
+```

+## Recursive tuple elements in `Iterable`
+
+We use the element type of `Iterable` when simplifying its intersection with a tuple. That
+simplification also preserves a recursive element type.

+from typing import Any, TypeVar
+from typing_extensions import TypeAliasType, assert_type

+T = TypeVar("T")

+A = TypeAliasType("A", "tuple[WithIterable[A], ...]")

+def f(x: A):

+## Recursive tuple elements in a protocol
+
+Each element of `A` must be both another `A` and an `Items`. We can inspect an element without
+expanding the tuple indefinitely, and an integer still fails that requirement.
+
+```py
+from collections.abc import Iterator
+from typing import Any, Protocol, assert_type
+from ty_extensions import Intersection
+
+class Items(Protocol):
+    def __iter__(self) -> Iterator[Any]: ...
+
+type WithItems[T] = Intersection[Items, T]
+type A = tuple[WithItems[A], ...]
+
+def f(x: A):
+    assert_type(x[0], WithItems[A])
+    y: int = x[0]  # error: [invalid-assignment]
+```
+
+## Recursive tuple elements in `Iterable`
+
+We use the element type of `Iterable` when simplifying its intersection with a tuple. That
+simplification also preserves a recursive element type.
+
+```py
+from collections.abc import Iterable
+from typing import Any, assert_type
+from ty_extensions import Intersection
+
+type WithIterable[T] = Intersection[Iterable[Any], T]
+type A = tuple[WithIterable[A], ...]
+
+def f(x: A):
+    assert_type(x[0], WithIterable[A])
+```
+
+## Boolean aliases after substitution
+
+Subtracting `True` from `bool` leaves only `False`. Using aliases for the arguments to `Minus` does
+not prevent that simplification.
+
+```py
+from typing import Literal
+from ty_extensions import Intersection, Not
+
+type Minus[T, U] = Intersection[T, Not[U]]
+type Boolean = bool
+type TrueLiteral = Literal[True]
+
+def f(x: Minus[Boolean, TrueLiteral]):
+    reveal_type(x)  # revealed: Literal[False]
+```

+### Recursive aliases and their complements
+
+For a fully static alias `A`, every object is either an `A` or not an `A`. This also holds when the
+alias refers to itself: the list element type `Not[A] | A` is `object`.
+
+```py
+from ty_extensions import Not
+
+type A = list[Not[A] | A]
+
+def f(x: A):
+    reveal_type(x[0])  # revealed: object
+```
+
+### Negated recursive aliases
+
+The list element is not an `A`. We can describe its type without expanding the recursive list each
+time it is inspected.
+
+```py
+from ty_extensions import Not
+
+type A = list[Not[A]]
+
+def f(x: A):
+    reveal_type(x[0])  # revealed: ~A
+```
+
+### Equivalent complements of a gradual recursive alias
+
+The presence of `Any` must not change what an alias means. Negating this recursive alias is
+equivalent to negating its definition. Generic inference respects that equivalence in either
+direction.
+
+```py
+from typing import Any, assert_type
+from ty_extensions import Not
+
+type A = list[tuple[Any, A]]
+
+def identity[T](x: T) -> T:
+    return x
+
+def f(x: Not[A], y: Not[list[tuple[Any, A]]]):
+    assert_type(identity(x), Not[list[tuple[Any, A]]])
+    assert_type(identity(y), Not[A])
+```

+## Applying `runtime_checkable`
+
+The `runtime_checkable` decorator can only be applied to protocol classes. Applying it to an
+ordinary class raises `TypeError` at runtime:
+
+```py
+from typing import Protocol, runtime_checkable
+
+# snapshot: invalid-argument-type
+@runtime_checkable
+class NotAProtocol: ...
+```
+
+```snapshot
+error[invalid-argument-type]: `runtime_checkable` can only be applied to protocol classes
+ --> src/mdtest_snippet.py:4:1
+  |
+4 | @runtime_checkable
+  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
+5 | class NotAProtocol: ...
+  |       ------------ `NotAProtocol` is not a protocol class
+info: A class is only a protocol if it directly inherits from `typing.Protocol` or `typing_extensions.Protocol`
+```
+
+The same restriction applies to `typing_extensions.runtime_checkable`:
+
+```py
+from typing_extensions import runtime_checkable as runtime_checkable_extensions
+
+# error: [invalid-argument-type]
+@runtime_checkable_extensions
+class AlsoNotAProtocol: ...
+```
+
+A subclass of a protocol is not itself a protocol unless it explicitly inherits from `Protocol`:
+
+```py
+class Base(Protocol): ...
+
+# error: [invalid-argument-type]
+@runtime_checkable
+class Concrete(Base): ...
+
+@runtime_checkable  # no diagnostic
+class Subprotocol(Base, Protocol): ...
+```
+
+## Calling `runtime_checkable` directly
+
+Direct calls enforce the same restriction, whether the class is passed by position or by name:
+
+```py
+from typing import Protocol, runtime_checkable
+from typing_extensions import runtime_checkable as runtime_checkable_extensions
+
+class NotAProtocol: ...
+class P(Protocol): ...
+
+runtime_checkable(NotAProtocol)  # error: [invalid-argument-type] "`runtime_checkable` can only be applied to protocol classes"
+runtime_checkable_extensions(cls=NotAProtocol)  # error: [invalid-argument-type]
+runtime_checkable(P)  # no diagnostic
+```
+
+## `runtime_checkable` in stub files
+
+In a stub file, a class can inherit from `Protocol` through an alias defined later in the file:
+
+```pyi
+from typing import runtime_checkable
+
+@runtime_checkable  # no diagnostic
+class P(ProtocolAlias): ...
+
+from typing import Protocol as ProtocolAlias
+```
+
+As in Python files, a subclass must explicitly inherit from `Protocol` to be a protocol:
+
+```pyi
+# error: [invalid-argument-type]
+@runtime_checkable
+class Concrete(P): ...
+```
+
+## `runtime_checkable` and decorator order
+
+Decorators are applied from bottom to top. An inner decorator can replace an ordinary class with a
+protocol before `runtime_checkable` receives it:
+
+```py
+from typing import Protocol, runtime_checkable
+
+class P(Protocol): ...
+
+@runtime_checkable  # no diagnostic
+@lambda cls: P
+class Replaced: ...
+```
+
+Reversing the order applies `runtime_checkable` to the ordinary class before it can be replaced:
+
+```py
+@lambda cls: P
+# error: [invalid-argument-type]
+@runtime_checkable
+class NotAProtocol: ...
+```
+
+An inner decorator can also replace a protocol with an ordinary class. `runtime_checkable` rejects
+the replacement:
+
+```py
+class Ordinary: ...
+
+# error: [invalid-argument-type]
+@runtime_checkable
+@lambda cls: Ordinary
+class ReplacedWithClass(Protocol): ...
+```
+
+If the inner decorator returns an integer, `runtime_checkable` rejects it because it is not a class:
+
+```py
+# error: [invalid-argument-type]
+@runtime_checkable
+@lambda cls: 1
+class ReplacedWithInstance(Protocol): ...
+```
